turns.prompt_text: How do I prevent my bamboo A1 printer from turning out like this? Attached 1 file. - cd30d132-3c08-4f12-84a0-bc7288560b63
turns.response_html:
It appears the print has suffered from a significant bed adhesion failure, causing the parts to detach and the printer to create the "spaghetti" seen in the image. This is a common hurdle, especially with multiple small, complex geometries like these vertebrae.

To ensure your next print remains firmly seated on the build plate, consider the following adjustments:

1. Build Plate Hygiene

The most frequent cause of detachment is oil from fingertips. Even a small amount of residue can prevent the first layer from bonding.

  • Wash with Dish Soap: Take the PEI plate to a sink and scrub it with warm water and basic dish soap (like Dawn). Dry it with a clean paper towel and avoid touching the print surface afterward.
  • Avoid IPA (Isopropyl Alcohol): While useful for quick wipes, IPA can sometimes just smear oils around on textured PEI rather than removing them entirely.

2. Slicer Settings for Stability

When printing tall or narrow objects, the nozzle can occasionally "snag" a part, knocking it over.

  • Add a Brim: In Bambu Studio, set the Brim Type to "Outer brim." This creates a wider base for each part, significantly increasing the surface area connected to the plate.
  • Enable Z-Hop: Ensure Z-Hop when retracting is enabled (usually under the "Extruder" or "Travel" tab). This lifts the nozzle slightly when moving between parts, preventing it from colliding with already printed sections.
  • Slow Down the First Layer: Reducing the "Initial Layer Speed" to 20–30 mm/s ensures a more methodical and secure bond.

3. Mechanical & Environmental Checks

  • Calibrate Bed Leveling: Ensure the "Auto Bed Leveling" (ABL) box is checked before hitting "Print." Even with a high-end sensor, a quick pre-print calibration is cheap insurance.
  • Check for Drafts: If the printer is near a vent or an open window, uneven cooling can cause the corners of the plastic to "curl" up (warping), which leads to the nozzle striking the part.
  • Auxiliary Fan: For small parts, sometimes the side cooling fan (Aux Fan) blows too hard, causing one side of the part to cool and shrink faster than the other. Try lowering the Aux Fan speed to 30-50% or turning it off for the first few millimeters.

4. Bed Temperature

Verify that your bed temperature is appropriate for the filament. For standard PLA on a textured PEI plate, a temperature of 60°C to 65°C is usually the "sweet spot" for maintaining adhesion throughout the duration of the print.

turns.prompt_text: This is a cool plate, Super Attack. Should I still wash it with Dawn dish soap? So
turns.response_html:
The SuperTack (often referred to as the "Super Attack") plate is actually specifically designed to address exactly what happened in your photo. It provides exceptionally strong adhesion, often requiring much lower bed temperatures than standard plates.

Regarding maintenance: Yes, you should still wash it with Dawn dish soap.

While the SuperTack surface is different from standard PEI, the fundamental enemy of 3D printing—finger oils—is the same. Here are a few specific tips for that plate:

Cleaning & Care

  • Dawn is the Gold Standard: Use warm water and regular Dawn. Avoid "hand soaps" or anything with moisturizers/lotions, as those will leave a film that kills adhesion.
  • Avoid Acetone: Never use acetone or harsh organic solvents on the SuperTack plate. It will chemically damage the special coating.
  • Soft Surface Warning: The SuperTack coating is softer than the textured PEI plates. Be very gentle with the metal scraper; it’s easy to gouge. If a print is stuck, let the plate cool completely, or put it in the freezer for 5 minutes—the parts usually pop right off once they contract.

Pro-Tips for the SuperTack Plate

  • Lower Your Temps: You can often run your bed at 35°C–45°C for PLA on this plate and still get perfect adhesion. If you run it at the standard 60°C, you might find it too hard to remove the parts.
  • The "Alcohol Trick": If a print is truly fused to the plate, drip a little Isopropyl Alcohol (IPA) around the edges of the print. The alcohol will wick underneath and help break the vacuum seal without you having to pry and scratch the plate.
  • No TPU: Avoid printing TPU directly on the SuperTack. It can bond so well that it peels the coating off when you try to remove it.

If you just gave it a good scrub with Dawn and still see those vertebrae sliding around, try adding a 5mm brim in Bambu Studio. It’ll give those small "feet" of the vertebrae a much wider anchor point.

How many grams of filament did that "spaghetti" accident cost you?

turns.prompt_text: I'm not sure but it looks like the air happened later on so it looks like everything stayed attached but as it got higher is when it messed up, I've had this happen before with things that get tall.
turns.response_html:
That observation is a classic sign of mechanical leverage at work. As the print gets taller, the part acts like a long lever; even a tiny bit of resistance or a "tap" from the nozzle at the top creates a massive amount of force at the base, snapping the part loose.

Since you mentioned this is a recurring issue with tall prints, here are the three most likely culprits for the Bambu A1 specifically:

1. Grid Infill (The Most Common Villain)

If you are using Grid infill, the nozzle actually crosses over its own paths on the same layer. This creates small "bumps" or intersections. As the print gets taller and the part starts to wobble slightly, the nozzle eventually catches one of these bumps, and the leverage knocks the part off the bed.

  • The Fix: Switch to Gyroid or Crosshatch infill. These patterns never cross themselves on the same layer, providing a much smoother path for the nozzle.

2. Excessive "Z-Wobble" or Part Sway

Tall, thin objects (like vertebrae stacked high) can start to vibrate or sway as the print head moves.

  • The Fix: Lower your Outer Wall Speed specifically for tall prints. Slowing down to 50–100 mm/s for the outer walls reduces the "jerk" motion that causes the part to oscillate.

3. "The Snag" (Z-Hop)

If your Z-hop isn't high enough, the nozzle might graze the top of the part during a travel move. On a short part, it’s a non-issue. On a tall part, it's a knockout blow.

  • The Fix: In Bambu Studio, go to your Printer Settings -> Extruder and increase the Z-hop when retracting to 0.4mm or 0.6mm. Also, ensure "Travel circumventing walls" is enabled so the nozzle avoids flying directly over the part when moving.

4. Support Stability

If those vertebrae require supports, make sure the supports themselves aren't failing. If a support pillar falls over mid-print, the next layer of the actual model will be printing into thin air, eventually creating a "blob" that the nozzle will collide with.

Quick Calibration Check: Since you are in Ames, if you've recently moved the printer or it's sitting on a desk that isn't perfectly stable, the vibration of the A1's high-speed movements could be contributing to that "sway." Placing the printer on a heavy concrete paver or a very solid workbench can make a world of difference for tall, delicate prints.

Are you printing these vertebrae as a single piece, or are they meant to be separate components for a larger assembly?

turns.prompt_text: Some of these parts really weren't that high before they fray like this, why not use gyroid at all times? Attached 1 file. - 338b06a8-e566-48dd-8d1a-a5f988759e1e
turns.response_html:
That is a very fair question. If Gyroid is objectively safer for tall or complex prints, why isn't it the default?

The short answer is: Speed and mechanical wear.

While Gyroid is excellent for preventing collisions, it has a few drawbacks that make it less "all-purpose" than patterns like Grid or the newer Crosshatch:

  • Printer "Shaking": Gyroid is a 3D wave pattern. It requires the printer's motors to constantly change direction in $x$ and $y$ simultaneously to create those curves. On an A1, this can cause the entire machine to vibrate significantly more than a straight-line pattern.
  • Print Time: Because the toolhead has to slow down slightly to navigate all those tiny curves, Gyroid usually adds about 5–10% to the total print time compared to Grid.
  • Mechanical Stress: Over thousands of hours, the constant rapid oscillation of Gyroid puts more wear on the belts and motors than the straight, high-speed lines of other infills.

Why your specific parts are "fraying" early

Looking at the new photo, those vertebrae have very organic, "overhanging" bits (the transverse processes).

If a part of the print sticks out into mid-air without enough support, the plastic can't stay "up." It droops, and the next layer has nothing to sit on, creating that bundle of "spaghetti" or fraying you see. Even if the part is only an inch tall, if the angle is too steep (usually over 55°–60°), it will fail without Supports.

A Modern Middle Ground: Crosshatch

If you want the safety of Gyroid without the vibrations and speed penalty, try the Crosshatch infill pattern in the latest version of Bambu Studio.

  • It is designed specifically to be "non-crossing" (like Gyroid), so the nozzle won't hit it.
  • It uses straight lines, so it prints much faster and quieter.

Try this for the next batch:

  1. Enable Tree Supports: Use "Tree (auto)" with the "Slim" or "Organic" style. This will prop up those "wings" on the vertebrae so they don't fray.
  2. Switch to Gyroid or Crosshatch: Since these parts have complex geometries, the "collision-free" nature of these patterns is worth the extra few minutes of print time.
  3. Check the "Overhangs" in the Slicer: Before you send the file, look at the preview. Any areas colored red are steep overhangs that might need those tree supports.

turns.prompt_text: Please explain to me the difference between gyroid cross hatch or the straight line.
turns.response_html:
Choosing the right infill is essentially a trade-off between structural integrity, printing speed, and machine longevity. On a high-speed machine like the A1, these differences become very apparent.

1. Grid (The "Straight Line" Standard)

This is often the default. It prints a simple grid of squares that stack directly on top of each other every layer.

  • How it works: It draws straight lines in one direction, then crosses over them in the other direction on the same layer.
  • The Conflict: Because it crosses over itself, it creates a small "bump" at every intersection. At high speeds, your nozzle can strike these bumps, which is likely what knocked your tall vertebrae over.
  • Best For: Simple, flat objects where speed is the priority and the nozzle doesn't have to travel over the part much.

2. Gyroid (The "Wavy" Non-Crossing Pattern)

Gyroid is a mathematically derived 3D shape that looks like a series of interlocking waves.

  • How it works: It never crosses its own path on the same layer. It creates a "pathway" that is equal in strength in every direction ($x, y, \text{ and } z$).
  • The Advantage: Since there are no "bumps" from crossing lines, the nozzle will almost never snag on the infill. It is also great for allowing air or fluids to pass through (it is "permeable").
  • The Downside: It forces your printer to vibrate rapidly to create the waves. You’ll hear your A1 "singing" or vibrating much louder.
  • Best For: Complex parts, tall/thin models, and parts that need to be strong from all angles.

3. Crosshatch (The Modern Hybrid)

This is a newer pattern designed specifically for high-speed "bed slingers" like your A1.

  • How it works: Like Gyroid, it is a non-crossing pattern. However, instead of using waves, it uses straight lines that shift slightly every layer to create a sturdy internal lattice.
  • The Advantage: You get the "snag-free" benefits of Gyroid, but because the lines are straight, the printer doesn't vibrate nearly as much. It is faster and quieter than Gyroid.
  • Best For: Almost everything. It is quickly becoming the "set it and forget it" choice for Bambu users who want to avoid nozzle collisions without the noise of Gyroid.

Comparison Table

FeatureGridGyroidCrosshatch
Nozzle Collision RiskHigh (Crosses itself)ZeroZero
Printing SpeedFastestSlowerFast
Vibration/NoiseLowHighLow
StrengthTop/Bottom heavyBalanced (Isotropic)Balanced

If you switch those vertebrae to Crosshatch or Gyroid, you'll likely find that the "fraying" and knocking-over issues disappear, as the nozzle will have a clear, bump-free path for the entire height of the print.

Since you're working with complex geometries like these, have you experimented with "Tree Supports" to help catch those overhanging edges?

turns.prompt_text: Could I have my bamboo printer slow down as it gets higher in layers? I wonder if it could be linear or logarithmic or something like that so that as it gets higher it gets slower but it doesn't really start slowing down until it gets like an inch off the board or something maybe half an inch
turns.response_html:
That is a very sophisticated approach to solving "bed-slinger" physics. As a tall part gains height, its moment of inertia increases, meaning the rapid back-and-forth movement of the bed is more likely to make the top of the part wobble like a pendulum.

While Bambu Studio doesn't have a single "Logarithmic Slowdown" slider, you can achieve this exact effect using Height Range Modifiers.

How to set up a Linear/Step Slowdown

You can tell the printer to change its behavior at specific heights. Here is how to implement your "inch off the board" rule:

  1. Right-click your model in the "Prepare" tab.
  2. Select Add Modifier -> Height Range Modifier.
  3. In the menu that appears on the left, set your Start Height (e.g., 25mm for ~1 inch) and End Height (the total height of your model).
  4. Switch to the Objects tab (instead of Global) and select that specific height range.
  5. Find the Speed settings. You can now manually lower the "Outer wall," "Inner wall," and "Infill" speeds for just that upper section.

Can it be "Automatic"?

If you want the printer to handle this dynamically without you math-ing out height ranges, there is a setting called Small Layer Cooling Time (under the Filament tab -> Cooling).

  • How it works: If a layer is very small (like the tip of a vertebra), the printer will automatically slow down to ensure the previous layer has cooled enough.
  • The Benefit: This naturally slows down the print as the geometry tapers off toward the top, which reduces the physical "jerk" on those delicate upper sections.

The Physics: Why Logarithmic?

Your intuition about a non-linear slowdown is spot on. The "wobble" doesn't increase linearly; it compounds as the center of gravity shifts upward.

$$F = m \cdot a$$

As the part gets taller, the acceleration ($a$) of the bed applies more torque to the base of the print. By slowing down the acceleration and jerk settings in those higher "Height Range Modifiers," you effectively neutralize that leverage.

A "Hardware" Workaround

If you find yourself printing tall items frequently in Ames, ensure your A1 is on the most rigid surface possible. If the table itself has any "give," the printer’s own vibrations will amplify the sway of a tall part. Some users even place a heavy paving stone under the printer to add mass and dampen those oscillations.

Since you've run into this a few times, would you like to look at how to adjust the Jerk settings specifically for those higher layers? It's often the sudden change in direction (jerk), rather than the top speed, that snaps a tall part off the plate.
